# Clinical Trials for Dogs with Cancer

Links last verified: August 20, 2026

## Explore Current Research Trials in Canine Oncology

When a beloved dog is diagnosed with cancer, many families ask whether a clinical trial may provide an additional option. Canine oncology studies are conducted throughout the United States and around the world, but identifying an appropriate trial, and participating in one, can sometimes be challenging.

Each clinical trial has specific eligibility requirements.

These may include: 

  * A dog’s breed
  * Age
  * Weight
  * Overall health
  * Life expectancy
  * Cancer type
  * Cancer stage
  * Previous care
  * ...and other medical factors

Meeting a study’s general description does not guarantee acceptance. Pet parents should speak directly with the research team and their veterinary care provider to determine whether a trial may be appropriate for their dog.

It is also important to understand that clinical trials are not always free.

Research funding may cover only certain tests, medications, procedures, or appointments. Families may still be responsible for additional veterinary expenses, travel, lodging, and repeated visits over several weeks or months, especially when a study is located far from home.

The following links are intended to help pet parents and veterinary professionals find information about current canine oncology trials being conducted throughout the United States and, in some cases, internationally.

We encourage families to carefully review each study’s eligibility requirements, location, potential costs, time commitment, and possible benefits and risks with their veterinary team.

## Start Here: Nationwide Search Tools

If you are not sure where to begin, start with the AVMA registry. It lets you search by cancer type and by location, which is faster than checking individual centers one at a time.

#### AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry

The AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry, formerly known as the AVMA Animal Health Studies Database, helps dog parents and veterinary professionals find veterinary clinical studies taking place throughout the United States and Canada. By making this information easier to access, the registry supports continued research and progress in veterinary medicine and canine health care.

If you are interested in a clinical trial for your dog, begin by discussing the study and your dog’s potential eligibility with your veterinary care provider.

 

AVMA Clinical Trials

#### National Cancer Institute, Comparative Oncology Program

The Comparative Oncology Program develops and conducts clinical trials in partnership with veterinary teaching institutions throughout the United States. Dogs enrolled in these studies receive care from board-certified veterinary oncologists committed to improving comfort, quality of life, and cancer care for companion animals.

The knowledge gained through this research may help advance the understanding of cancer and support future progress in both canine and human oncology.

National Cancer Institute

#### PetCure Oncology

PetCure Oncology provides stereotactic radiation surgery and stereotactic radiation therapy, commonly known as SRS and SRT. These highly precise forms of radiation therapy have been used in human oncology and are now available for dogs with certain types of cancer.

PetCure Oncology reports using SRS and SRT in thousands of companion animals with a variety of tumor types. Its affiliated veterinary specialists continue to study these approaches to better understand their potential benefits, safety considerations, side effects, and appropriate applications in canine cancer care.

PetCure Oncology Clinical Trials

#### ACI Biosciences

Network conducting trials at participating private practices.

## Keep in Mind

Clinical trials may explore new approaches to diagnosing or supporting dogs with cancer. These may include chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgical procedures, temperature-based therapies, immunotherapy, photodynamic therapy, and other emerging approaches.

Although many clinical trials take place at veterinary colleges and teaching hospitals, a growing number of specialty and referral practices also participate in canine cancer research. Some studies require every appointment to be completed at the participating institution, while others may allow certain tests, procedures, or follow-up visits to be handled by a dog’s regular veterinary team.

The words “experimental” and “investigational” can understandably feel concerning. Before a new therapy or procedure reaches a veterinary clinical trial, researchers have typically completed earlier stages of evaluation. However, unknowns may remain regarding its safety, effectiveness, or potential side effects. A study is offered because researchers believe the approach may provide meaningful benefits, but participation does not guarantee a positive outcome.

Pet parents should review the study’s purpose, requirements, possible benefits, known and unknown risks, costs, and available alternatives with the clinical trial team and their dog’s veterinary care provider before making a decision.

# Comparative Oncology (Canine Trials and Resources)

Image: A physician and assistant examine a dog patient at the University of Minnesota

Credit: University of Minnesota

Enlarge Image

As in humans, cancers in pet dogs arise spontaneously. Dogs also have similar genomes, immune responses, living environment, and tumor complexity to humans. Studying pet dogs in cancer research, including in clinical trials, can provide valuable information for the development of future treatments for people.

The Integrated Canine Data Commons

The Integrated Canine Data Commons (ICDC) is a node in the larger NCI human Cancer Research Data Commons (CRDC). The Division of Cancer Treatment and Diagnosis (DCTD) developed the publicly available and searchable ICDC to incorporate genomic, proteomic, imaging, clinical trial, biomarker, population study, cancer model, and immuno-oncology data. This enables comparative analysis with tumors that arise spontaneously in pet dogs and advances research on human cancers.

PRECINCT Research Network: PRE-medical Cancer Immunotherapy Network Canine Trials 

In 2017, NCI granted five teams U01 awards (RFA-CA-17-001) and one team a U24 award (RFA-CA-17-002) to perform canine immunotherapy trials and correlative analyses. In 2022, the program was renewed with U01 awards (RFA-CA-21-050) issued to five new universities and a U24 award issued to the same team as in 2017 (RFA-CA-21-051). 
 
Learn more about the PRECINCT Network. 

Contact: Connie Sommers, PhD (sommersc@mail.nih.gov)

Immuno-oncology Canine Clinical Trials

DCTD is developing novel immuno-oncology agents for use in clinical trials involving pet dogs with cancer to inform, optimize, and better understand the underlying biology and administration of these agents in human patients. These canine-specific reagents target promising immune regulatory proteins. They will be useful not only as therapeutics, both as monotherapies and in combination with other cancer treatments, but also for pharmacodynamic assays and as imaging agents.

This multi-year, multi-phase, coordinated project is a collaboration between DCTD and the NCI Center for Cancer Research Comparative Oncology Program (COP). It leverages the COP’s veterinary clinical trial infrastructure (Comparative Oncology Trials Consortium) to advance the DCTD canine drug development pipeline. Newly developed agents will ultimately be shared with the extramural comparative oncology community to further cancer research.

Longitudinal Studies in Dogs with Cancer

The purpose of these studies is to obtain longitudinal tumor specimens that can be analyzed to inform our understanding of the molecular basis of canine cancer progression. In addition, this work will help determine whether pet dogs are a reliable model for evaluating the effectiveness of investigational therapeutics and treatment regimens for potential future use in humans.

Goals

  * Expand molecular studies to understand treatment and resistance throughout the development and evolution of malignant disease using pet dogs as a model

Objectives

  * To longitudinally track individual dogs that may receive treatments and/or participate in clinical trials or receive no treatment at the request of the owner (to study the natural history of the cancer in molecular detail)
  * To collect annotated canine cancer patient clinical/trial history and molecular characterization of biopsy material and blood at time of diagnosis, post-treatment, and at relapse. These will be used to to determine whether and in what circumstances naturally occurring tumors arise in dogs. They are good models of human cancer, tumor response, development of resistance to therapeutic regimens, and disease progression

title: Pathology foundation models for training-free case retrieval in salivary gland tumors
snippet:
[wordlim: 200] Published: 2 days ago; 
Title: Pathology foundation models for training-free case retrieval in salivary gland tumors
Authors: Maximilian J. Roesel, Niklas Kiermeyer, Philipp Keyl, Frederick Klauschen
Date: Thu Oct 15 15:40:48 2026

In pathology, pattern recognition relies on a frame of reference built through extensive training and experience, which may still fall short when encountering rare cancer subtypes. Archives of previously diagnosed tumors often contain relevant precedents, yet identifying the most relevant cases remains challenging. Here we explore whether content-based retrieval with current pathology foundation models facilitates rare cancer diagnostics without any task-specific training. Pathologists can query a digitized archive using a region of interest (ROI) from a whole slide image (WSI) and retrieve morphologically similar cases, along with their ICD-O codes and corresponding WSIs. The ROI can be selected manually or automatically using a gated attention-based multiple instance learning model. We evaluate our approach by leave-one-case-out on an imbalanced dataset of 137 salivary gland tumor cases spanning 12 ICD-O morphology categories, comparing four pathology foundation models (Atlas2, Atlas2-B, Atlas2-S, and UNI2h). Top-1/3/5 retrieval was 62.5%/76.7%/81.3% for Atlas2, 50.2/66.6/72.9% for UNI2h, 52.3%/71.5%/77.6% for Atlas2-B and 54.4/65.2/73.7% for Atlas2-S. Macro-averaged F1 ranged from 69.0% for the smallest model Atlas2-S to 76.6% for the largest model Atlas2 across the five classes with at least ten cases. Our modified Chamfer similarity separated correct from incorrect matches among the Top-5 more reliably for Atlas2 (AUC 0.754) than for Atlas2-B (0.679, p = 0.020) and Atlas2-S (0.653, p = 0.003), but not UNI2h (0.697, p = 0.196). Requiring no additional training or manual annotation, this approach makes departmental archives searchable with pathology foundation models, providing a low-barrier route to case-based differential diagnosis and extending the individual frame of reference to the collective experience of the department.

Purpose : To develop and evaluate CAPTOR, a deep-learning vision-language foundation model for oncologic chest-abdomen-pelvis (CAP) CT interpretation. Materials & Methods : CAPTOR (Chest-Abdomen-Pelvis foundaTion model for Oncologic Radiology) is a contrastive vision-language model, trained using a pretraining strategy for oncologic CAP CT (in single- or multiple-series acquisitions), on a multicenter retrospective dataset from North America, Europe and Asia, predominantly from tumor lesion examinations. CAPTOR was compared with state-of-the-art CT foundation models on three downstream tasks: disease detection, survival prediction using TumorImagingBench and image retrieval. Classification and retrieval were both evaluated on held-out internal and public test sets, stratified by anatomical coverage and indication.

title: From Adults to Children: Benchmarking Foundation Models for Chest X-Ray Classification under Domain Shift
snippet:
[wordlim: 200] Published: 2 days ago; 
Title: From Adults to Children: Benchmarking Foundation Models for Chest X-Ray Classification under Domain Shift
Authors: Sara Inácio, Hugo Proença, João C. Neves
Date: Thu Oct 15 12:57:08 2026

Foundation models have shown significant potential across diverse fields and have been applied to medical imaging, but their robustness across patient populations remains unclear. In this work, we investigate foundation models' ability to generalize from adult to pediatric chest X-ray classification. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first benchmark to compare multiple foundation models under a common adult-to-pediatric evaluation setting while also analyzing the effect of adaptation depth. We harmonize VinDr-CXR and PediCXR into a five-label classification task and evaluate six foundation models and two CNN baselines. All models are adapted using adult data only and tested in both the in-domain and pediatric domains using linear probing, partial fine-tuning, and full fine-tuning. The benchmark reveals a clear and consistent trend: all models suffer a substantial performance degradation when transferred from adult to pediatric data, with drops exceeding 10 percentage points. While Macro-AUROC values reach approximately 92% on the adult test set, performance decreases to around 78% on the pediatric domain. Another important finding is that increasing the depth of adaptation does not significantly improve cross-population generalization. Moreover, strong in-domain performance does not translate into better performance on pediatric data.

أكد العالم المصرى الدكتور مصطفى السيد أنه يتم حاليا التواصل مع وزارة الصحة بصفة مستمرة لعرض نتائج تجارب استخدام جزيئات الذهب النانومترية فى علاج السرطان والرد على كافة استفساراتها، والتأكد من أن تلك الجزيئات لا تؤثر سلبيا على خلايا الجسم السليمة، لإقرار تلك الطريقة والبدء فى تطبيقها على البشر.

جاء ذلك خلال المحاضرة التى ألقاها الدكتور السيد، اليوم الأحد، فى الصالون العلمى لأكاديمية البحث العلمى والتكنولوجيا لعرض أحدث تطورات أبحاثه فى علاج السرطان بجزيئات الذهب النانومترية، وبدء إجراء تجارب سريرية لهذا النوع من العلاج، بحضور عدد كبير من طلاب الكليات العلمية والصيادلة ونخبة من أساتذة الجامعات والمراكز البحثية.

وعرض العالم المصرى فكرة علاج السرطان بجزيئات الذهب النانومترية القائمة على حقن قطع الذهب الصغيرة (نانو) داخل الجسم لتمتص الضوء تحت الأحمر وتسخن الخلية السرطانية للقضاء عليها، موضحا أن التجارب أثبتت أنه عقب تسخين قطع ذهب ورفع درجة الحرارة حول الخلية يتم انصهار أو "تسييح" الخلايا السرطانية والبروتينات حولها مما يمنع انتشارها فى باقى أجزاء الجسم، مؤكدا أن التجارب مستمرة لمعرفة طريقة تغير عمل الخلية السرطانية بعد اعتيادها على تلك الطريقة.

# Treatment for Latent Tuberculosis Infection

## Key points

People with latent tuberculosis (TB) infection can be treated to prevent TB disease. CDC and the National Tuberculosis Coalition of America preferentially recommend short-course, rifamycin-based, 3- or 4-month latent TB infection treatment regimens.

Image: Doctor Showing Prescription to Female Patient

## Overview

### Guidelines

Guidelines for the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection: Recommendations from the National Tuberculosis Controllers Association and CDC, 2020

Finding and treating people with latent TB infection (sometimes called inactive TB for non-clinical audiences) is essential for controlling and eliminating TB disease. Treatment for latent TB infection prevents TB disease.

For Everyone: Treating Inactive Tuberculosis

## Treatment Considerations for Latent TB infection

‎People with latent TB infection should be treated to prevent the development of TB disease. Progression from untreated latent TB infection to TB disease accounts for approximately 80% of U.S. TB cases.

Do not start latent TB infection treatment until TB disease is excluded.

People with known risk factors for developing TB disease (once infected with TB bacteria) and have a positive TB blood test (interferon-gamma release assay or IGRA) result, or a tuberculin skin test (TB skin test) result should be given high priority for latent TB infection treatment.

CDC and the National Tuberculosis Coalition of America preferentially recommend short-course, rifamycin-based, 3- or 4-month latent TB infection treatment regimens over 6- or 9-month isoniazid monotherapy. Short-course regimens are effective, safe, and have higher completion rates than longer regimens.

Treatment for latent TB infection can be administered by directly observed therapy (in-person or video) or by self-administered therapy.

# Breast Cancer Treatment Options

There's no one-size-fits-all treatment for breast cancer. Your healthcare team will rely on your pathology report to advise you on your treatment options.

Written by [Button: Abby Curtis] & [Button: Jamie DePolo]|Reviewed by [Button: Kevin Fox, MD]|Updated on June 4, 2026

In this article

Planning your treatment

Adjuvant and neoadjuvant treatments

Surgery

Chemotherapy

Radiation therapy

Hormonal therapy

Targeted therapy

Immunotherapy

Complementary therapy

Clinical trials

Research on treatment presented at conferences

Sponsor Message

Sponsor Message

Shortly after you’re diagnosed with breast cancer, you  meet with your doctor and possibly other members of your healthcare team to decide which of the many available breast cancer treatment options are right for you. 

Sponsor Message

## Planning your treatment

Sponsor Message

Each case of breast cancer is unique, which is why understanding your pathology report is so important for you and your doctor to put together a treatment plan. 

Sponsor Message

Your treatment plan is made up of one or more specific therapies to treat the breast cancer and reduce the risk of the cancer coming back (also called recurrence).

Sponsor Message

If you have questions or doubts about your diagnosis or proposed treatment plan, you should never hesitate to get a second opinion. While a second opinion may confirm your original doctor’s diagnosis, another doctor may also be able to provide more details about the type and stage of the breast cancer, raise additional treatment options you hadn’t considered, or recommend a different course of action.

Sponsor Message

This is also a good time to reach out to palliative care, also sometimes called supportive care. Unlike hospice, palliative care can be used at any stage of treatment to help with planning your care and managing symptoms. In fact, the earlier in your treatment course you start, the more helpful it can be.

Sponsor Message

## Adjuvant and neoadjuvant treatments

Sponsor Message

In many — but not all — cases, surgery is the first treatment for breast cancer.

Sponsor Message

Treatments given before surgery are called neoadjuvant treatments.  For example, many people receive chemotherapy before surgery. Neoadjuvant treatments help shrink the cancer so surgery may be less extensive. The response to neoadjuvant treatments can help doctors decide which treatments, if any, are needed after surgery.

## New cancer treatments for dogs in 2026

Veterinary oncology is shifting toward more precise, less disruptive treatments designed to protect healthy tissue and preserve your dog’s quality of life.

Take a look at why targeted and injectable radiation therapies are on the rise as a new cancer treatment for dogs — and why the benefits outweigh more traditional therapies.

### Targeted Radiation Therapy

Unlike traditional radiation that passes through the body, targeted radiation treatments are delivered directly to the tumor. This approach allows:

  * High effectiveness against cancer cells
  * Minimal exposure to surrounding healthy tissue
  * Fewer treatment sessions

This innovative therapy is especially helpful for tumors in sensitive areas like the face, legs, or near vital organs.

### Injectable cancer treatment

Targeted radiation therapy involves injecting therapeutic agents directly into the tumor. This injection is designed to:

  * Destroy cancer cells from the inside out
  * Reduce the need for repeated anesthesia
  * Shorten recovery times

For many dogs, this means less stress and a quicker return to normal routines.

### Minimally Invasive Alternatives to Surgery

When surgery isn’t an option — or when cancer returns after surgery — minimally invasive treatments can help manage or eliminate tumors without major procedures.

These options are particularly beneficial for:

  * Older dogs
  * Dogs with other health conditions
  * Tumors that are difficult to fully remove surgically

Take a look at some new radiation therapies for dogs below. These options provide alternatives to chemotherapy for dogs, offering minimally invasive cancer treatment for pets.

### Examples of targeted radiation therapy in veterinary medicine

Several modern radiation approaches focus on delivering higher precision while protecting healthy tissue, including:

  * Stereotactic Radiation Therapy (SRT or SBRT) – This method delivers very precise, high-dose radiation over just a few sessions instead of weeks. It is often used for brain tumors, nasal tumors, and other hard-to-reach cancers. Treatment is typically available at large specialty or university referral hospitals.

Koebel, Renata Ivanek, Parminder Basran, Jennifer Sun, Casey Cazer, Gayatri Anil, Tommaso Banzato, Liz Barton, Dottie Cimino Brown, Leszek Bukowski, Marta Castelhano, Simon Coghlan, Christopher De Sa, Nikki Dutta, Hala Ghali, Julio Giordano, Joshua Glass, David C. Hogg, Nicholas Hollingshead, Adam Kiehl, Ziang Liu, Monica Meduri, Param Mohapatra, Kim Nayyer, Amelia Nelson, Peter-John Mantyla Noble, Christopher Pinard, Beryl Rabindran, Scott Ross, Ron Seccia, Moira Sheehan, Fei Wang, Tracy L. Webb, Kilian Q. Weinberger, Heather M. Whitney, Chen Xin
Date: Fri Oct  9 15:41:38 2026

VETNET represents an ecosystem of live benchmark datasets and evaluation frameworks designed to accelerate AI-driven innovation in animal science and veterinary medicine through standardized, high-quality datasets and multi-institutional collaboration across academic and non-academic sectors. This framework addresses the gap between AI advances in human medicine and the fragmented state of veterinary AI development.

title: Modeling the Microenvironmental Dynamics of Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma in Lacrimal Gland with Treatment Intervention
snippet:
[wordlim: 200] Published: 4 days ago; 
Title: Modeling the Microenvironmental Dynamics of Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma in Lacrimal Gland with Treatment Intervention
Authors: Ayasa Akter, Miss Sajnin Binta Salam Efty, Uzzwal Kumar Mallick
Date: Tue Oct 13 11:51:17 2026

Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) of the lacrimal gland is a rare and extremely life threatening malignant tumor with a high risk of recurrence and poor long-term outcomes. On the other hand, due to its complex molecular dynamics and low incidence rate, treatment strategies are very limited. In this study, a mathematical model is developed based on the biological phenomena of the tumor microenvironment using nonlinear ordinary differential equations. It is analyzed both analytically and numerically. According to the findings, the growth of tumor cells is associated with the depletion of oxygen and nutrients, while severe hypoxia promotes the development of abnormal blood vessels and makes tumor control more difficult. Surgery and postoperative radiotherapy have been considered as treatment strategies, and we have observed that surgery alone may not be sufficient to prevent the regrowth of residual tumor cells. In addition, postoperative radiotherapy provides better control of the residual tumor burden, particularly when the remaining tumor cells have higher radiosensitivity. Furthermore, different radiotherapy interruption scenarios have been investigated, and the results indicate that longer gaps between radiotherapy doses can adversely affect the overall treatment response, leading to increased overall toxicity and a higher number of residual tumor cells at the end of the observation period. Consequently, our results suggest that postoperative radiotherapy after surgery, combined with adequate radiosensitivity of the residual tumor cells and adherence to the prescribed treatment schedule without prolonged interruptions, may reduce the risk of tumor recurrence and potentially improve long term survival.

title: Morphology-aware deep learning predicts colorectal cancer survival from whole-slide images
snippet:
[wordlim: 200] Published: 5 days ago; 
Title: Morphology-aware deep learning predicts colorectal cancer survival from whole-slide images
Authors: Hikmat Khan, Metin N. Gurcan, Anil Parwani, Wendy L. Frankel, Wei Chen, Muhammad Khalid Khan Niazi
Date: Tue Oct 13 02:22:42 2026

Background: Five-year survival prediction from hematoxylin-and-eosin whole-slide images could support risk stratification, but the task is weakly supervised, and the tissue morphologies carrying prognostic information remain incompletely characterized. Methods: We conducted a retrospective secondary analysis using TCGA-COAD/READ (n=562) for morphology-specific analysis, Alliance/ CALGB 89803 (n=424) for model development, and SurGen (n=218) for external evaluation. We propose MorphContrast, a morphology-aware contrastive multiple-instance learning framework that uses tissue labels as structural supervision for five-year survival prediction. MorphContrast combines gated-attention pooling with three auxiliary objectives: patch-level morphology labels define within-patient contrasts, outcome concordance or discordance defines cross-patient contrasts within matched morphologies, and diversity regularization discourages representational collapse. Morphology-matched patches from patients with discordant outcomes serve as hard negatives, encouraging prognostic discrimination within comparable histologic contexts. Results: Morphology-specific models show weak but distributed prognostic discrimination: adipose tissue achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.622, stroma achieves 0.604, and both perform comparably to tumor epithelium (0.601-0.605). On Alliance/CALGB 89803, the single model achieves an AUC of 0.642, while the post hoc ensemble reaches a pooled out-of-fold AUC of 0.70 and a risk-group hazard ratio of 3.79 (95% confidence interval: 2.55-5.63). On the external SurGen colon cancer cohort (n=218), the single model and ensemble achieve AUCs of 0.669 and 0.678, respectively. Conclusions: These findings support tissue morphology as structural supervision for outcome-aware representation learning in colorectal cancer prognosis.

title: Pathology foundation models for training-free case retrieval in salivary gland tumors
snippet:
[wordlim: 200] Published: 2 days ago; 
Title: Pathology foundation models for training-free case retrieval in salivary gland tumors
Authors: Maximilian J. Roesel, Niklas Kiermeyer, Philipp Keyl, Frederick Klauschen
Date: Thu Oct 15 15:40:48 2026

In pathology, pattern recognition relies on a frame of reference built through extensive training and experience, which may still fall short when encountering rare cancer subtypes. Archives of previously diagnosed tumors often contain relevant precedents, yet identifying the most relevant cases remains challenging. Here we explore whether content-based retrieval with current pathology foundation models facilitates rare cancer diagnostics without any task-specific training. Pathologists can query a digitized archive using a region of interest (ROI) from a whole slide image (WSI) and retrieve morphologically similar cases, along with their ICD-O codes and corresponding WSIs. The ROI can be selected manually or automatically using a gated attention-based multiple instance learning model. We evaluate our approach by leave-one-case-out on an imbalanced dataset of 137 salivary gland tumor cases spanning 12 ICD-O morphology categories, comparing four pathology foundation models (Atlas2, Atlas2-B, Atlas2-S, and UNI2h). Top-1/3/5 retrieval was 62.5%/76.7%/81.3% for Atlas2, 50.2/66.6/72.9% for UNI2h, 52.3%/71.5%/77.6% for Atlas2-B and 54.4/65.2/73.7% for Atlas2-S. Macro-averaged F1 ranged from 69.0% for the smallest model Atlas2-S to 76.6% for the largest model Atlas2 across the five classes with at least ten cases. Our modified Chamfer similarity separated correct from incorrect matches among the Top-5 more reliably for Atlas2 (AUC 0.754) than for Atlas2-B (0.679, p = 0.020) and Atlas2-S (0.653, p = 0.003), but not UNI2h (0.697, p = 0.196). Requiring no additional training or manual annotation, this approach makes departmental archives searchable with pathology foundation models, providing a low-barrier route to case-based differential diagnosis and extending the individual frame of reference to the collective experience of the department.

title: What Is Cancer? - NCI
snippet:
[wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Aug 28, 2026 — Explanations about what cancer is, how cancer cells differ from normal cells, and genetic changes that cause cancer to grow and spread.
## 

Differences between Cancer Cells and Normal Cells

Get email updates from NCI on cancer health information, news, and other topics

Cancer cells differ from normal cells in many ways. For instance, cancer cells:

  * grow in the absence of signals telling them to grow. Normal cells only grow when they receive such signals.
  * ignore signals that normally tell cells to stop dividing or to die (a process known as programmed cell death, or apoptosis).
  * invade into nearby areas and spread to other areas of the body. Normal cells stop growing when they encounter other cells, and most normal cells do not move around the body.
  * tell blood vessels to grow toward tumors.  These blood vessels supply tumors with oxygen and nutrients and remove waste products from tumors.
  * hide from the immune system. The immune system normally eliminates damaged or abnormal cells.
  * trick the immune system into helping cancer cells stay alive and grow. For instance, some cancer cells convince immune cells to protect the tumor instead of attacking it.
  * accumulate multiple changes in their chromosomes, such as duplications and deletions of chromosome parts. Some cancer cells have double the normal number of chromosomes.
  * rely on different kinds of nutrients than normal cells. In addition, some cancer cells make energy from nutrients in a different way than most normal cells. This lets cancer cells grow more quickly. 

Many times, cancer cells rely so heavily on these abnormal behaviors that they can’t survive without them. Researchers have taken advantage of this fact, developing therapies that target the abnormal features of cancer cells. For example, some cancer therapies prevent blood vessels from growing toward tumors, essentially starving the tumor of needed nutrients.  

Image

Cancer is a disease caused when cells divide uncontrollably and spread into surrounding tissues.

Enlarge Image

Image

Immune system cells can detect and attack cancer cells. But some cancer cells can avoid detection or thwart an attack. Some cancer treatments can help the immune system better detect and kill cancer cells.

Enlarge Image

## 

How Does Cancer Develop?

Cancer is a genetic disease—that is, it is caused by changes to genes that control the way our cells function, especially how they grow and divide.

Genetic changes that cause cancer can happen because:

  * of errors that occur as cells divide.
  * of damage to DNA caused by harmful substances in the environment, such as the chemicals in tobacco smoke and ultraviolet rays from the sun. (Our Cancer Causes and Prevention section has more information.)
  * they were inherited from our parents. 

The body normally eliminates cells with damaged DNA before they turn cancerous. But the body’s ability to do so goes down as we age. This is part of the reason why there is a higher risk of cancer later in life.

Each person’s cancer has a unique combination of genetic changes. As the cancer continues to grow, additional changes will occur. Even within the same tumor, different cells may have different genetic changes.

Image: Diagram showing a breakdown of DNA structure, going from nucleus and cell to showing the chromosome and the parts that make up DNA, including genes and nucleotides.

Cancer is caused by certain changes to genes, the basic physical units of inheritance. Genes are arranged in long strands of tightly packed DNA called chromosomes.

Credit: © Terese Winslow

Enlarge Image

Image

Cancer is caused by changes to DNA. Most cancer-causing DNA changes occur in sections of DNA called genes. These changes are also called genetic changes.

Enlarge Image

Image: Infographic titled "What Causes Genetic Changes?" showing a silhouette of a person in the center. Surrounding the silhouette are six icons with labels: "Heredity" with a DNA strand, "Viruses" with virus cells, "UV Radiation" with a sun, "Smoking" with a cigarette, "Chemicals" with a chemical bottle, and "Cells Dividing" with dividing cells. Each icon points towards the silhouette.

Genetic changes that cause cancer can be inherited or arise from certain environmental exposures. Genetic changes can also happen because of errors that occur as cells divide.

Credit: National Cancer Institute

Enlarge Image

Image

Most often, cancer-causing genetic changes accumulate slowly as a person ages, leading to a higher risk of cancer later in life.

Enlarge Image

## 

Types of Genes that Cause Cancer

Image

A DNA change can cause genes involved in normal cell growth to become oncogenes. Unlike normal genes, oncogenes cannot be turned off, so they cause uncontrolled cell growth.

Enlarge Image

The genetic changes that contribute to cancer tend to affect three main types of genes—proto-oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, and DNA repair genes. These changes are sometimes called “drivers” of cancer.

Proto-oncogenes are involved in normal cell growth and division. However, when these genes are altered in certain ways or are more active than normal, they may become cancer-causing genes (or oncogenes), allowing cells to grow and survive when they should not.

Tumor suppressor genes are also involved in controlling cell growth and division. Cells with certain alterations in tumor suppressor genes may divide in an uncontrolled manner.

DNA repair genes are involved in fixing damaged DNA. Cells with mutations in these genes tend to develop additional mutations in other genes and changes in their chromosomes, such as duplications and deletions of chromosome parts. Together, these mutations may cause the cells to become cancerous.

As scientists have learned more about the molecular changes that lead to cancer, they have found that certain mutations commonly occur in many types of cancer. Now there are many cancer treatments available that target gene mutations found in cancer. A few of these treatments can be used by anyone with a cancer that has the targeted mutation, no matter where the cancer started growing.

Image: A graphic of showing the difference between a normal cell and a caner cell.

 In normal cells, tumor suppressor genes prevent cancer by slowing or stopping cell growth. DNA changes that inactivate tumor suppressor genes can lead to uncontrolled cell growth and cancer.

Enlarge Image

Image

Each person’s cancer has a unique combination of genetic changes. Specific genetic changes may make a person’s cancer more or less likely to respond to certain treatments.

Enlarge Image

## 

When Cancer Spreads

Image: Drawing that shows metastasis, when a primary cancer spreads from its first location to other parts of the body.

In metastasis, cancer cells break away from where they first formed and form new tumors in other parts of the body. 

Credit: © Terese Winslow

Enlarge Image

A cancer that has spread from the place where it first formed to another place in the body is called metastatic cancer. The process by which cancer cells spread to other parts of the body is called metastasis.

Metastatic cancer has the same name and the same type of cancer cells as the original, or primary, cancer. For example, breast cancer that forms a metastatic tumor in the lung is metastatic breast cancer, not lung cancer.

Under a microscope, metastatic cancer cells generally look the same as cells of the original cancer. Moreover, metastatic cancer cells and cells of the original cancer usually have some molecular features in common, such as the presence of specific chromosome changes.

Within a tumor, cancer cells are surrounded by a variety of immune cells, fibroblasts, molecules, and blood vessels—what’s known as the tumor microenvironment. Cancer cells can change the microenvironment, which in turn can affect how cancer grows and spreads.

Enlarge Image

Image

Cancer cells can break away from the original tumor and travel through the blood or lymph system to distant locations in the body, where they exit the vessels to form additional tumors. This is called metastasis.

title: Morphology-aware deep learning predicts colorectal cancer survival from whole-slide images
snippet:
[wordlim: 200] Published: 5 days ago; 
Title: Morphology-aware deep learning predicts colorectal cancer survival from whole-slide images
Authors: Hikmat Khan, Metin N. Gurcan, Anil Parwani, Wendy L. Frankel, Wei Chen, Muhammad Khalid Khan Niazi
Date: Tue Oct 13 02:22:42 2026

Background: Five-year survival prediction from hematoxylin-and-eosin whole-slide images could support risk stratification, but the task is weakly supervised, and the tissue morphologies carrying prognostic information remain incompletely characterized. Methods: We conducted a retrospective secondary analysis using TCGA-COAD/READ (n=562) for morphology-specific analysis, Alliance/ CALGB 89803 (n=424) for model development, and SurGen (n=218) for external evaluation. We propose MorphContrast, a morphology-aware contrastive multiple-instance learning framework that uses tissue labels as structural supervision for five-year survival prediction. MorphContrast combines gated-attention pooling with three auxiliary objectives: patch-level morphology labels define within-patient contrasts, outcome concordance or discordance defines cross-patient contrasts within matched morphologies, and diversity regularization discourages representational collapse. Morphology-matched patches from patients with discordant outcomes serve as hard negatives, encouraging prognostic discrimination within comparable histologic contexts. Results: Morphology-specific models show weak but distributed prognostic discrimination: adipose tissue achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.622, stroma achieves 0.604, and both perform comparably to tumor epithelium (0.601-0.605). On Alliance/CALGB 89803, the single model achieves an AUC of 0.642, while the post hoc ensemble reaches a pooled out-of-fold AUC of 0.70 and a risk-group hazard ratio of 3.79 (95% confidence interval: 2.55-5.63). On the external SurGen colon cancer cohort (n=218), the single model and ensemble achieve AUCs of 0.669 and 0.678, respectively. Conclusions: These findings support tissue morphology as structural supervision for outcome-aware representation learning in colorectal cancer prognosis.

title: HexaBee-4B: Six-Language Translation with Multilingual Answering and Bidirectional Supervision
snippet:
[wordlim: 200] Published: 5 days ago; 
Title: HexaBee-4B: Six-Language Translation with Multilingual Answering and Bidirectional Supervision
Authors: Iman Barati, Mohammadmostafa Rostamkhani, Mohammad Badzohreh
Date: Mon Oct 12 08:15:08 2026

Multilingual translation requires a model to preserve meaning while producing text in a requested language. We present HexaBee-4B, a translator adapted from Gemma 3 4B IT through three stages: Wikipedia continued pretraining, joint multilingual answering and answer-text translation, and bidirectional translation specialization. The intermediate stage connects two tasks through shared multilingual answers: answering a question in the requested language and translating an answer into that language. It comprises 19.46 million answering records, including 5.76 million cross-language question-answer pairs, and 10.70 million answer-text translations. The final stage uses 658,274 forward and reverse synthetic translation examples. On 36,572 synthetic test examples spanning all 30 directions among Arabic, Chinese, English, Hebrew, Persian, and Spanish, HexaBee-4B achieves direction-macro chrF++ of 73.75, compared with 57.11 for Gemma 3 4B IT and 66.83 for Gemma 3 12B IT. BLEU, TER, COMET, and a matched model-judged subset support the same overall ranking. These results demonstrate improved translation across the six-language set, with chrF++ gains in every evaluated direction over both baselines.

title: ChemArgus: Automated Scientific Diagnostics for Lab-Grade Multimodal Chemistry Reasoning: A Frontier Benchmark
snippet:
[wordlim: 200] Published: 3 days ago; 
Title: ChemArgus: Automated Scientific Diagnostics for Lab-Grade Multimodal Chemistry Reasoning: A Frontier Benchmark
Authors: Hanyao Guo, Mo Cui, Zihan Tan, Leixin Sun, Yichun Wang, Yinan Shen, Guojun Zhu, Jia Jiang, Erhao Chen, Zui Chen, Wenzhe Gao, Zhihao Yu, Qijun Wang, Yetian Zhu, Jiande Chen, Chuhang Pei, Yao Jiang, Yichen Fan, Pinhan Wang, Xiaorui Pan, Qianyi Zhu, Yang Liu, Mang Ye, Guancheng Wan
Date: Wed Oct 14 11:24:56 2026

Chemistry evaluation has moved past multiple-choice probes toward open-ended expert problems, yet the benchmarks that define the current frontier still score answer endpoints alone. Such scoring conflates memorized facts with stepwise derivation, treats visual and textual inputs as interchangeable, and confounds long-horizon planning with stepwise execution. These blind spots prevent any diagnosis of where the reasoning chain breaks in a model. We present ChemArgus, a competition-level chemistry benchmark drawn from chemistry competition material, textbooks, and research papers, whose scoring replaces the answer endpoint with three measurement properties.

title: VETNET: Assembling Benchmark Datasets for AI-Driven Veterinary Innovation
snippet:
[wordlim: 200] Published: last week; 
Title: VETNET: Assembling Benchmark Datasets for AI-Driven Veterinary Innovation
Authors: Katherine J. Koebel, Renata Ivanek, Parminder Basran, Jennifer Sun, Casey Cazer, Gayatri Anil, Tommaso Banzato, Liz Barton, Dottie Cimino Brown, Leszek Bukowski, Marta Castelhano, Simon Coghlan, Christopher De Sa, Nikki Dutta, Hala Ghali, Julio Giordano, Joshua Glass, David C. Hogg, Nicholas Hollingshead, Adam Kiehl, Ziang Liu, Monica Meduri, Param Mohapatra, Kim Nayyer, Amelia Nelson, Peter-John Mantyla Noble, Christopher Pinard, Beryl Rabindran, Scott Ross, Ron Seccia, Moira Sheehan, Fei Wang, Tracy L. Webb, Kilian Q. Weinberger, Heather M. Whitney, Chen Xin
Date: Fri Oct  9 15:41:38 2026

VETNET represents an ecosystem of live benchmark datasets and evaluation frameworks designed to accelerate AI-driven innovation in animal science and veterinary medicine through standardized, high-quality datasets and multi-institutional collaboration across academic and non-academic sectors. This framework addresses the gap between AI advances in human medicine and the fragmented state of veterinary AI development.

title: EHR-Bench: A Chinese Multi-Task Benchmark for Recruitment AI
snippet:
[wordlim: 200] Published: 5 days ago; 
Title: EHR-Bench: A Chinese Multi-Task Benchmark for Recruitment AI
Authors: Ruijia Yang, Bing Xu, Zulong Chen, Zhipeng Xu, Jia Xu, Yipeng Yu, Ying Zhou, Zeyi Wen
Date: Mon Oct 12 12:27:33 2026

Recruitment applications span diverse operations, from drafting job descriptions and interpreting queries to organizing profiles, assessing fit, and recommending candidates and jobs. Systematic LLM evaluation therefore requires task coverage that reflects this range of business needs. We introduce EHR-Bench, an open Chinese benchmark comprising twelve tasks across six capability families and five recruitment scenarios. The tasks cover generation, extraction, classification, retrieval, semantic similarity, and reciprocal ranking within one evaluation framework. An internal recruitment dataset guides task definitions, the occupation taxonomy and sampling targets, output requirements, and scoring protocols. Following these specifications, we construct 8,336 task instances from public materials and controlled augmentation, with source-aware expert review and documented provenance. We evaluate twelve LLMs through task-level, capability-level, and aggregate comparisons. Closely ranked models exhibit distinct task strengths, and performance varies across input sources, reference evidence, and candidate pools. Five shared models retain the same observed Overall ordering on a private operational reference, with variation in capability and task correspondence. EHR-Bench provides a reproducible foundation for systematic model assessment, task-specific model selection, and further research on LLMs for recruitment. The project repository is available at https://github.com/EhrBench/EHR-Bench.

title: bharatSetu: a 1M x 22 bridge for indic translation
snippet:
[wordlim: 200] Published: 6 days ago; 
Title: bharatSetu: a 1M x 22 bridge for indic translation
Authors: Haq Nawaz Malik, Nahfid Nissar, Faizan Iqbal
Date: Sun Oct 11 15:39:19 2026

India's Eighth Schedule recognises 22 languages, yet parallel data is uneven across them, and many language pairs, especially among lower-resource languages such as Bodo, Dogri, Santali and Kashmiri, lack direct bitext. We present BharatSetu 22-Indic 1M, a row-aligned table of 984,764 English sentences, each paired with machine translations into all 22 scheduled languages (21,664,808 Indic cells), generated with the sarvamai/sarvam-translate model family. Because every Indic cell in a row translates the same English sentence, any two columns form a translation pair: 462 directed Indic-to-Indic pairs, or 506 including English, without direct bitext. We call these pivot-derived pairs and propose a confidence layer that lets users choose how strictly each pair is connected. The corpus is machine-generated and not human-verified; quality is expected to vary by language, domain and sentence style, and pivot-derived pairs can inherit errors from both sides. We therefore release BharatSetu as a machine layer and propose a human-correction layer keyed to the same row identifiers, so that each corrected column upgrades every pair that uses it, together with an evaluation protocol. We report no translation-quality results.

title: CT25: the new generation of CTEQ-TEA PDFs
snippet:
[wordlim: 200] Published: 3 days ago; 
Title: CT25: the new generation of CTEQ-TEA PDFs
Authors: Alim Ablat, Daniel Adamiak, Aurore Courtoy, Sayipjamal Dulat, Yao Fu, Marco Guzzi, T. J. Hobbs, Joey Huston, Maximiliano Ponce Chavez, Kirtimaan Mohan, Pavel Nadolsky, Tanishq Sharma, Dan Stump, Keping Xie, C. -P. Yuan
Date: Wed Oct 14 21:07:36 2026

This contribution reviews CT25, a new generation of CTEQ--TEA parton distribution functions (PDFs) for precision QCD. With its first member sets released in 2025, the CT25 family addresses common uses of parton distributions in diverse contexts. We describe the CTEQ--TEA Parton Cloud, an online database of exploratory global fits to precision QCD measurements, from which we select PDF solutions for general- and special-purpose calculations. These solutions are published as complementary error PDF ensembles---the baseline CT25, CT25m, CT25pd, and ensembles with conservative priors---optimized for distinct uses. They implement new approaches to quantifying uncertainties and different treatments of theoretical, parametrization, and nuclear-target uncertainties. In particular, they provide complementary frameworks for exploring PDF uncertainties at large partonic momentum fractions relevant to HL-LHC and EIC studies. Further details will appear in the forthcoming CT25 publication.

title: BaT-SAM: Introducing Inductive Bias into SAM via a Mixture of Convolutional Experts for Brain Tumor Segmentation
snippet:
[wordlim: 200] Published: last week; 
Title: BaT-SAM: Introducing Inductive Bias into SAM via a Mixture of Convolutional Experts for Brain Tumor Segmentation
Authors: Sumiaya Jannat, Md Mahedi Hasan, Md Shamimul Islam, Md Nur Hossain
Date: Sun Oct 11 04:09:35 2026

Accurate brain tumor segmentation from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for diagnosis and treatment planning; however, manual delineation is labor-intensive and time-consuming. Existing approaches are either task-specific with limited generalization or rely on user-provided prompts during inference. We present BaT-SAM, a parameter-efficient adaptation framework that enables fully automatic brain tumor segmentation with the Segment Anything Model (SAM). BaT-SAM injects local inductive bias into SAM's frozen Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder via Conv-LoRA, where image features are processed by a sparsely gated mixture of multi-scale convolutional experts. This design compensates for the limited translation-equivariant inductive bias of vanilla ViTs while fine-tuning fewer than 5M parameters (less than 1% of the full model). To remove the need for user prompts, we further introduce a lightweight self-prompting box regressor that is jointly optimized with the adapter using scheduled sampling and predicts tumor locations directly from image embeddings. On the BRISC2025 benchmark, BaT-SAM achieves a weighted mean IoU of 0.832 while outperforming state-of-the-art benchmarks. It further demonstrates strong cross-dataset generalization, achieving Dice scores of 0.702 on Figshare and 0.784 on the LGG MRI Segmentation dataset.

Title: VETNET: Assembling Benchmark Datasets for AI-Driven Veterinary Innovation
Authors: Katherine J. Koebel, Renata Ivanek, Parminder Basran, Jennifer Sun, Casey Cazer, Gayatri Anil, Tommaso Banzato, Liz Barton, Dottie Cimino Brown, Leszek Bukowski, Marta Castelhano, Simon Coghlan, Christopher De Sa, Nikki Dutta, Hala Ghali, Julio Giordano, Joshua Glass, David C. Hogg, Nicholas Hollingshead, Adam Kiehl, Ziang Liu, Monica Meduri, Param Mohapatra, Kim Nayyer, Amelia Nelson, Peter-John Mantyla Noble, Christopher Pinard, Beryl Rabindran, Scott Ross, Ron Seccia, Moira Sheehan, Fei Wang, Tracy L. Webb, Kilian Q. Weinberger, Heather M. Whitney, Chen Xin
Date: Fri Oct  9 15:41:38 2026

VETNET represents an ecosystem of live benchmark datasets and evaluation frameworks designed to accelerate AI-driven innovation in animal science and veterinary medicine through standardized, high-quality datasets and multi-institutional collaboration across academic and non-academic sectors. This framework addresses the gap between AI advances in human medicine and the fragmented state of veterinary AI development.

title: PET Quantification-Preserving Registration for Longitudinal Whole-Body PSMA PET/CT
snippet:
[wordlim: 200] Published: 2 days ago; 
Title: PET Quantification-Preserving Registration for Longitudinal Whole-Body PSMA PET/CT
Authors: Fryderyk Kögl, Anna Reithmeir, Daniel M. Lang, Emily Chan, Rickmer Braren, Julia A. Schnabel
Date: Thu Oct 15 07:54:21 2026

We adapt the diffeomorphic coarse-to-fine LapIRN architecture for longitudinal whole-body PSMA PET/CT registration in the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg challenge. The method combines affine pre-registration, multi-modal deformable registration, and test-time instance optimization. We further introduce PET biomarker preservation losses for metabolic tumor volume (MTV) and total lesion glycolysis (TLG), including Jacobian-based constraints, and a per-structure rigidity regularization for skeletal structures. The submitted configuration achieved 81.0% DSC and 6.17 mm HD95, with MTV and TLG errors of 3.3% and 3.3%, respectively, on our evaluation protocol. Code is available at https://github.com/koegl/psmareg.

title: Women and the Nobel Prize in the sciences: an update to 2026
snippet:
[wordlim: 200] Published: 4 days ago; 
Title: Women and the Nobel Prize in the sciences: an update to 2026
Authors: Per Lunnemann, Liselotte Jauffred
Date: Tue Oct 13 15:50:54 2026

Every October, the Nobel Prizes in Physics, Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine and Economic Sciences are announced, with one to three prizes in each discipline. Of the 769 Laureates (since 1901) in these four disciplines only 4% are women (30 Laureates). In 2026, there are eight Laureates within these disciplines and they are all men. Based on historical data across four fields and a Bayesian hierarchical model, we update the 8 year old model on bias in Nobel Prizes and confirm the gender gap, with exceedingly large confidence.

# Clinical Trials for Dogs with Cancer

Links last verified: August 20, 2026

## Explore Current Research Trials in Canine Oncology

When a beloved dog is diagnosed with cancer, many families ask whether a clinical trial may provide an additional option. Canine oncology studies are conducted throughout the United States and around the world, but identifying an appropriate trial, and participating in one, can sometimes be challenging.

Each clinical trial has specific eligibility requirements.

These may include: 

  * A dog’s breed
  * Age
  * Weight
  * Overall health
  * Life expectancy
  * Cancer type
  * Cancer stage
  * Previous care
  * ...and other medical factors

Meeting a study’s general description does not guarantee acceptance. Pet parents should speak directly with the research team and their veterinary care provider to determine whether a trial may be appropriate for their dog.

It is also important to understand that clinical trials are not always free.

Research funding may cover only certain tests, medications, procedures, or appointments.

title: SurvICL: a Foundation Model for in-context Survival Analysis
snippet:
[wordlim: 200] Published: 2 days ago; 
Title: SurvICL: a Foundation Model for in-context Survival Analysis
Authors: Julie Alberge, Linus Bleistein, Judith Abécassis, Marine Le Morvan, Gaël Varoquaux, David Holzmüller
Date: Thu Oct 15 17:16:56 2026

Tabular foundation models (TFMs) now outperform gradient-boosted trees in classification and regression. Yet in survival analysis, which predicts when an event occurs from censored data, often on small clinical cohorts, we find that no existing TFM beats the half-century-old Cox model. We address this issue by introducing SurvICL, a TFM that predicts survival curves in-context. SurvICL is pretrained on purely synthetic datasets generated from a novel flexible proportional-odds prior that outperforms other prior types in our ablation study. Unlike most other survival models, SurvICL is trained with a plain quantile regression loss, which is possible because its synthetic pre-training data generator can provide uncensored event times. Additionally, we introduce the largest survival benchmark to date spanning 103 datasets. On the 63 datasets held out from all design decisions, SurvICL outperforms 20 tree-based, deep, and foundation-model baselines without any tuning: it wins 82.9\% of pairwise comparisons in integrated Brier score, against 71.3\% for the runner-up, the Cox model, and is the first model to rank above Cox on small datasets.

#### Anivive Wins Full U.S. FDA Approval for Laverdia, First At-Home Oral Treatment for Canine Lymphoma

30 June 2026 | Tuesday | News

* * *

Full approval validates Anivive's AI-enabled drug development platform, with Laverdia becoming the first FDA-approved product developed through the company's drug repurposing and AI-driven clinical trial model while advancing global regulatory expansion.

Image

* * *

  * Anivive converts Laverdia-CA1 to full FDA approval
  * First FDA-approved product to validate Anivive's AI-enabled development model — from drug repurposing through clinical trial enrollment
  * Affordable oral lymphoma treatment administered at home
  * Additional approvals underway in Australia, Brazil, Canada, Europe, Japan and the United Kingdom

Anivive Lifesciences announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Center for Veterinary Medicine has granted full approval for Laverdia® (verdinexor tablets), marking a major advancement in the treatment of canine lymphoma. Laverdia is the first FDA-approved oral, at-home treatment for lymphoma in dogs designed to give veterinarians and pet owners a safe, effective, and more accessible option for managing one of the most common cancers in dogs.

Laverdia also marks the first FDA-approved product to complete Anivive's technology-enabled development cycle. AniviveSELECT, the company's AI drug repurposing platform, identified and prioritized verdinexor for canine lymphoma by connecting evidence from human medicine with veterinary disease biology. AniviveTRIAL then helped identify, match and recruit dogs for the nationwide pivotal study, contributing approximately 40% of enrollment, accelerating the path to approval.

# New scanning technology trialled for prostate cancer patients

by Samantha Rey

11 March 2025

Image: PET CT Scan

The PSMA PET/CT trial will scan up to 1000 men in the UK.

A new kind of scan that could be key to improving the treatment of high-risk prostate cancer is about to be tested in a new £1.89 million clinical trial led by Professor Hash Ahmed and funded by Prostate Cancer UK.

But it is unclear if PSMA PET/CT definitively sees all of the cancer spread and can enable more accurate treatment decisions by identifying men with aggressive, or high-risk prostate cancer. The AVIDITY trial will test this once and for all, following men for longer than previous trials.

Led by Professor Hashim Ahmed from Imperial College London, the trial will recruit men from over 30 centres around the UK. The trial is also being co-led by Mr Martin Connor and Professor Tara Barwick from Imperial College London, as well as Professor Rhian Gabe and Dr Adam Brentnall from Queen Mary University of London.

They will randomly divide the men with high-risk prostate cancer into two groups. One will receive treatment based on what the current standard imaging tests (CT scan and bone scan) show.  The other group will receive the treatment based on the findings of the new PSMA PET/CT scan. Up to 1000 men will be recruited for the trial. Both groups will have their cancer treatment decisions made based on the imaging results they receive.

title: Fast, flexible, and first-in-brain: how the 5G trial is taking on glioblastoma
snippet:
[wordlim: 100] Published: 11 months ago; Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; We're funding a pioneering new trial to find more and better treatment options for people with glioblastoma brain tumours.
Despite better understanding, patients with glioblastoma – a fast-growing form of brain cancer – have been left in limbo, with few new treatment options in recent decades. But a pioneering new clinical trial – 5G – is set to offer more options to UK patients and kick-start progress.

Brain tumours are devastating. As well as affecting a person’s ability to walk or move, or communicate, they can take away what makes people who they are – their self-identity.

Another issue is how drugs are tested for safety before reaching patients. Most toxicology studies are done in animals with an intact blood–brain barrier – the natural defence that prevents many substances from entering the brain. Because of this, many promising drugs are dismissed as unable to reach brain tumours. But in patients with brain tumours, the barrier is often damaged, meaning more drugs may be able to get through than once thought. In fact, growing evidence from people with cancer that has spread to the brain shows that a range of treatments, from standard chemotherapy to targeted therapies and antibody-based drugs, can work effectively there.

Yet people with primary brain tumours are still routinely excluded from early clinical trials that test new drugs for the first time in humans. This cautious approach has meant lost opportunities to discover which experimental treatments might actually help them.

### Study enrolls dogs with urothelial carcinoma to assess anti-cPD-L1 monoclonal antibody (mAb) safety and efficacy, with potential applications for human treatments.

The Purdue University College of Veterinary Medicine, in partnership with Akston Biosciences Corporation, has initiated the enrollment of dogs with urinary bladder cancer in a clinical trial of a pioneering immunotherapy. The immunotherapy consisting of an anti-cPD-L1 monoclonal antibody (mAb) is designed to target and block the cPD-L1 protein on cancer cells. This, in turn, is expected to enhance the immune system’s ability to attack the cancer cells more effectively to improve outcomes and extend life.

title: Helping Dogs—and Humans—with Cancer: NCI’s Comparative Oncology Studies
snippet:
[wordlim: 100] Published: 7.3 years ago; Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; NCI's comparative oncology programs support clinical trials for pet dogs with cancer, which may provide insights into new treatments for...
Since 2003, NCI has been using information from studies of canine cancer to help guide studies of human cancer and vice versa—a field known as comparative oncology. Two NCI efforts, the Comparative Oncology Program (COP) and the Pre-medical Cancer Immunotherapy Network for Canine Trials (PRECINCT), facilitate trials of new therapies for different types of cancer in pet dogs, as well as laboratory studies to learn more about the basics of canine cancer.

“Pet dogs benefit from what we do because we learn about their cancer and that can ultimately help identify better treatments for them,” said Amy LeBlanc, D.V.M., director of the Comparative Oncology Program in NCI’s  Center for Cancer Research. “We see the work that we do as an opportunity to help both dogs and people.”

How to Enroll Your Dog in an NCI-Supported Trial

If your dog has cancer and you are interested in enrolling him or her in an NCI-funded clinical trial, please call or email the contact person listed on the following pages:

NCI-Funded Canine Immunotherapy Trials Network

Comparative Oncology Program Open Clinical Trials

Humans and pet dogs share the same living spaces, so they are exposed to some of the same environmental factors that cause cancer. Plus, cancer in both species can take years to develop, and in many cases, its growth is often driven by similar genetic mutations.

Because of these important similarities, studying pet dogs with naturally occurring cancers provides researchers with valuable clues about human cancer, Dr. LeBlanc said. Comparative oncology studies offer a different perspective than studies of artificially created cancers in lab animals such as mice and rats, she added.

Although no animal can perfectly model exactly how a drug will act in humans, some scientists believe that studies in dogs may provide a better indicator of a drug’s potential in humans than studies in other animals.

Image

Unleashing Comparative Oncology

Dr. Nicola Mason of the University of Pennsylvania School of Veterinary Medicine describes using comparative oncology approaches to research immunotherapy in both dogs and humans.

In 2015, for example, an NCI-supported trial tested an experimental drug called NHS-IL12 in pet dogs with melanoma. The study determined the drug’s optimal dose, side effects, how it is absorbed and broken down, and confirmed its mechanism of action. It also showed that the drug partially shrank the tumors of two dog patients.

## Bringing Cancer Researchers Together

Another great thing about NCI’s comparative oncology programs is that they bring researchers together, said Dr. London. The veterinary oncology community “was relatively siloed,” she said, but these programs “connected it, and allowed people to communicate and collaborate.”

The programs connect researchers who study cancer in pet dogs with those who study the disease in humans, said Dr. Hecht. “This is probably the first time that there’s been a concerted effort to pull veterinary oncologists into the larger cancer research community,” she added.

Author(s)Abi Bautista-Alejandre, Assistant Editor

Fact checked by: Yasmeen Qahwash

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) may progress to feline small cell gastrointestinal (GI) lymphoma, researchers say. Texas A&M University is testing a new treatment option for the cancer.

Developing slowly over months to years, feline small cell gastrointestinal (GI) lymphoma can be difficult to detect.^{1} With this type of cancer resembling many of the common digestive issues cats often experience, understanding the disease, warning signs, diagnosis, and treatment is important to ensure the well-being of feline patients with chronic GI symptoms.

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and small cell GI lymphoma are thought to be closely related, representing different stages of the same underlying process.

title: What Is Cancer? - NCI
snippet:
[wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Aug 28, 2026 — Explanations about what cancer is, how cancer cells differ from normal cells, and genetic changes that cause cancer to grow and spread.
Many times, cancer cells rely so heavily on these abnormal behaviors that they can’t survive without them. Researchers have taken advantage of this fact, developing therapies that target the abnormal features of cancer cells. For example, some cancer therapies prevent blood vessels from growing toward tumors, essentially starving the tumor of needed nutrients.  

Image

Cancer is a disease caused when cells divide uncontrollably and spread into surrounding tissues.

Enlarge Image

## 

How Does Cancer Develop?

Cancer is a genetic disease—that is, it is caused by changes to genes that control the way our cells function, especially how they grow and divide.

Genetic changes that cause cancer can happen because:

The body normally eliminates cells with damaged DNA before they turn cancerous. But the body’s ability to do so goes down as we age. This is part of the reason why there is a higher risk of cancer later in life.

Each person’s cancer has a unique combination of genetic changes. As the cancer continues to grow, additional changes will occur. Even within the same tumor, different cells may have different genetic changes.

Genetic changes that cause cancer can be inherited or arise from certain environmental exposures. Genetic changes can also happen because of errors that occur as cells divide.

Credit: National Cancer Institute

Enlarge Image

Image

Most often, cancer-causing genetic changes accumulate slowly as a person ages, leading to a higher risk of cancer later in life.

Enlarge Image

## 

Types of Genes that Cause Cancer

Image

A DNA change can cause genes involved in normal cell growth to become oncogenes. Unlike normal genes, oncogenes cannot be turned off, so they cause uncontrolled cell growth.

Enlarge Image

The genetic changes that contribute to cancer tend to affect three main types of genes—proto-oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, and DNA repair genes. These changes are sometimes called “drivers” of cancer.

Current Term Enrollment Estimates (CTEE) series is published every January and May, providing final enrollment estimates for the fall and spring terms. It provides national enrollment estimates by credential type, institutional sector and other characteristics (e.g., locale, program focus), enrollment intensity, student demographics (e.g., age, race/ethnicity, gender), and major field, as well as state-level enrollment estimates. The Current Term Enrollment Estimates report differs from the Stay Informed report series which is designed to quantify the effects of COVID-19 by analyzing year-over-year percent change in unadjusted preliminary data for fixed panels of institutions that reported data in the same month each year across all comparison years. Hence, enrollment estimates may differ between the CTEE and the Stay Informed reports due to the difference in methodology and institution coverage.

## Research That Saves Lives

What does it take to outsmart cancer? Research. We’ve invested more than $5 billion in cancer research since 1946, all to find more – and better – treatments, uncover factors that may cause cancer, and improve cancer patients’ quality of life.

Surveillance & Health Equity Science We CONDUCT and publish research on cancer prevention, surveillance, health services, and disparities. Publications include Cancer Facts & Figure reports. 

Population Science We CONDUCT and publish research about cancer risk factors, the quality of life, and cancer survivors through Cancer Prevention Studies (CPS), including CPS-II and CPS-3.

Extramural Discovery Science We FUND high impact and innovative research for any type of cancer and from bench to bedside by supporting scientists across the United States with research grants.

Dual Enrollment lets you earn college credit while still in high school or while completing your GED.

## For High School Students

Dual enrollment provides students the unique opportunity to take community college classes while still in high school.

Dual enrollment enables high school students to take college courses, taught by college professors, at their high school campus. These courses can also count toward your high school diploma, allowing students to get a head start on their higher education goals.

For assistance, contact DualEnrollment@CCCCO.edu,

Look up enrollment in Wiktionary, the free dictionary.

Enrollment (American spelling) or enrolment (British spelling) may refer to:

  * Matriculation, the process of initiating attendance to a school
  * The act of entering item into a roll or scroll.
  * The total number of students properly registered and/or attending classes at a school (see List of largest universities by enrollment)
  * Concurrent enrollment, the process in which high school students enroll at a university or college usually to attain college credit
  * The participation of human subjects in a clinical trial
